questions.questionText: Bring out the causes of persistent high food inflation in India and suggest measures for ensuring long-  term price stability.
questions.subject: Economy

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by defining inflation and giving a brief background of the persistent high food inflation in India.
• In the body, first bring out the causes for the same.
• Next, suggest measures for ensuring long term price stability.
• Conclude by emphasizing their synergy and link to SDGs. | | --- | **Inflation** is the **rate of increase in prices** of goods and services in an economy over a given period of time. Economic Survey (2024-25) points out the **persistence in inflation**, particularly food inflation. Food inflation **surged after the pandemic** to 6.4 per cent on average (between 2020-21 and 2023-24), higher than the 5.9 per cent overall CPI inflation. **Fig. Comparison of retail and food inflation** (Jan 2024-Jan 2025). Experts have cited the **following factors** as being responsible for the **persistent high food inflation** in India: 1. a) rise in prices of **vegetables and pulses** which combinedly hold a high **weightage** (8.99%) in overall CPI basket; b) increase in **international prices** of cereals (wheat) and **fertilizers** due to the impact of **geopolitical conflicts** (Russia-Ukraine war). 2. a) Lower harvest in **price-sensitive commodities** (onion) in major **producing regions** (Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Gujarat) due to **uneven monsoon**; b) damage to **horticultural crops** due to **unseasonal** **pre-monsoonal rainfall,** which also trigger **temporary storage and transportation problems**. 3. a) Highly **perishable** nature of certain commodities (tomato); b) **temporal and spatial** concentration of production (tur dal in Maharashtra and Karnataka) makes it susceptible to **regional issues and** **supply chain** constraints; c) **limited potential for import** during periods of shortage due to India’s status as a **major producer** (pointed out by Economic Survey 2024-25). Ensuring **long-term price stability** India requires a mix of **following** measures such as:. 1. **Controlling artificial scarcity:** a) prevent hoarding by strengthening **Essential Commodities Act,** b) strict enforcement of **stock limits** c) improve **real-time price monitoring** using digital tools. 2. **Enhancing productivity:** a) promoting **high-yield seeds, precision farming, efficient irrigation** (drip, sprinkler) b) **crop diversification (**crop rotation, intercropping) for risk sharing. c) expand **storage** **infrastructure** to reduce post-harvest losses d) Strengthening **food processing capabilities (**PM FME) to stabilize supply throughout the year. 3. **Reforming agricultural market:** a) strengthening **e-NAM** to ensure better price discovery b) expanding **DBT** for fertilizers subsidies to reduce production cost c) flexible **MSP and procurement** **policy** that adjusts to production levels d) exploring a **stable agri-EXIM policy regime** to ensure sustained availability of products. Managing persistent high food inflation requires **comprehensive measures** including **supply-side** **interventions, market reforms**, and **sustainable agriculture** to balance consumer affordability with farm income stability. ***(401 words)***

questions.questionText: “Fiscal policy can serve as a cornerstone for sustainable development”. In light of this statement,  discuss the significance of fiscal policy in a developing economy like India.
questions.subject: Economy

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by defining fiscal policy.
• In the body, discuss the significance of fiscal policy in a developing economy like India.
• Conclude by highlighting the importance of deficit management and coordination with monetary policy for sustainable development. | | --- | Fiscal policy refers to the government's use of **expenditure and revenue measures** to influence various aspects of the national economy- levels of **economic activity, employment, price stability,** etc. In a developing country like India, fiscal policy holds **immense significance**, especially in **ensuring** **sustainable development,** as discussed: 1. Enhancing people’s **disposable incomes** and **standard of living** through **wealth redistribution** and reducing **income inequality. (SDG 10)** a. **Income support** schemes (PM-KISAN) and provision of b**asic goods and services** through dedicated schemes (PMAY, NFSA). b. a) Reduction in **personal income taxes**; b) **progressive taxation** policies (higher proportion of direct tax) and generational **wealth redistribution** (wealth tax, inheritance tax); c) access to **basic** **goods and services** (lower GST on items of mass consumption). 2. Provides fiscal stimulation and enhances **economic competitiveness** through infrastructural and industrial development (**SDG 9**). a. a) Capital expenditure** (11,11,111cr for 2024-25) creates a crowd**-in effec**t for private investment;** b) support for the **manufacturing sector** (PLIs) and enhancing **job creation** (ELIs) c) **strategic disinvestment policy** to optimize **resource allocation** (Air India, BPCL disinvestment) and improve **efficiency**. b. a) Tax incentives** for **infrastructure development** (Section 80IA deductions, infrastructure bond benefits);** b) **targeted tax measures** to boost industrial growth (corporate tax cuts) and **entrepreneurship** (abolition of angel tax); c) **infrastructure-specific levies** (infrastructure cess) to fund development projects. 3. Provision for **social support system. (SDG 3,4,6):** a. a) Expenditure on **public health** infrastructure, **education** infrastructure (PM-Shri Schools) leading to better health (reduced MMR) and education outcomes (near 100% GER in primary education); b) **social security** through dedicated schemes (NSAP, One Rank One Pension). b. a) Building **health and education services** (health and education cess); b) allocation from the **Universal Service Obligation Fund** to improve **digital infrastructure** and connectivity in underserved areas. 4. Furthering **inclusive growth** and **human development**. (**SDG 1,2,6**) a. a) **Gender equity** through gender-responsive budgeting and supportive institutions (One Stop Centres) b) empowerment of **vulnerable sections** of society (PM JANMAN) c) **poverty alleviation** measures (MGNREGA) and schemes for **nutritional security** (PM POSHAN). b. a) Tax incentives for women** (lower stamp duty on women owned properties);** b) agricultural promotion by **exempting agricultural income** from tax. 5. Promote **desirable consumption** patterns to achieve **sustainable growth**. (**SDG 7,11,12**) a. a) Access to **clean energy** sources (PM Ujjwala Yojana; PM Surya Ghar Bijli), reducing **carbon** **footprint** (FAME scheme). b. a) **Sin tax** on energy generation from fossil fuels (clean energy cess on coal); b) **excise and** **customs relief** to increase availability of components for renewable energy projects (solar panels); c) **green financing instruments** (Green Bonds). India's developmental journey (**Viksit Bharat 2047**) requires balancing **growth with equity**. Within a framework of **prudent deficit management** (FRBM Act), and complemented by appropriate **monetary policy**, fiscal measures create an **enabling environment** for **inclusive** and **sustainable development**. (***454 words***)

questions.questionText: Amid global economic uncertainties, India’s Balance of Payments (BoP) has shown remarkable  resilience. Elaborate on the factors contributing to this stability.
questions.subject: Economy

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by giving a brief background of global economic uncertainties and India’s external sector resilience.
• In the body, discuss the factors contributing to India’s Balance of Payments (BoP) stability.
• Conclude by providing suggestions to maintain this stability. | | --- | As per **Global Economic Policy Uncertainty Index**, the world faces rising political and economic uncertainty due to **geopolitical conflicts (**Russia-Ukraine war, West Asia conflict), **geoeconomic fragmentation (**trade wars), and **extreme climate events** (heatwaves). The **2024 "Great Election Year"** (affecting over half the world's population) added to **policy unpredictability**. Amidst these global economic uncertainties, India’s Balance of Payments (BoP) has shown remarkable **resilience.** This is on account of the following **factors**: 1. a) Stable current account deficit** despite increase in merchandise trade deficit (due to rise in net services receipt);** b) substantial **private transfers (**with remittances reaching $31.9 billion in Q2 FY25), reflecting the **economic resilience** of the Indian diaspora. 2. a) **FDI inflows have remained resilient** (YoY growth ~18% till Nov 2024) driven by India’s **robust** **economic fundamentals**, ongoing **structural reforms (**GST rationalization), and growing consumer base; b) **reversal** of the trend of **FPI outflows** and **upward trend in** External Commercial Borrowing **(ECBs)** due to long-term attractiveness of Indian equity markets (highlighted by ES 2024-25). 3. a) **Low external debt-to-GDP ratio** (19.4% in Sept 2024) and a **decline** in the share of **short-term debt** therein (19.4% to 18.8% between June to Sept 2024); b) high **forex reserves** (~$654billion, March 2025), providing **buffer** against external shocks. 4. a) **Inclusion of Indian Bonds** in **Global Indices** (JP Morgan Index) boosted foreign investment and capital inflows; c) growth in **NRI deposits** (owing to favourable exchange rate environment), further strengthening reserves. 5. a) Long-term measures** aimed at promoting **export competitiveness** (RoDTEP scheme, Dak Niryat Kendras) and enhanced **market access** (trade agreements with UAE, Australia);** b) efforts aimed at **reducing import dependence** (SPRs, renewable energy push, NMEO-Oilseeds). Amid **uncertainties over global trade policies** (e.g., potential tariff wars under the new U.S. administration), India must safeguard BoP stability. This can be achieved by adopting a **strategic trade roadmap** aimed at enhancing export competitiveness, reducing import dependence, and **deepening global supply chain** **integration.** ***(317 words)*** **RoDTEP:** Remission of Taxes and Duties on Exported Products**; SPR:** Strategic Petroleum Reserves**; NMEO-** **Oilseeds:** National Mission on Edible Oils- Oilseeds

questions.questionText: The economic reforms of 1991 significantly reshaped India’s economic landscape. Elaborate on the  need for these reforms and their key objectives.
questions.subject: Economy

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by giving a brief background about the economic reforms of.
• In the body, first elaborate on the need for these reforms, and then discuss their key objectives. Conclude by highlighting the need for Reforms. | | --- | The economic reforms of 1991 entailed an **overhaul** of Indian economy in alignment with **market principles.** They marked a departure from the **post-independence economic model** (socialistic pattern, import substitution) towards the IMF-sponsored **Structural Adjustment Programme.** **Need** for these reforms arose due to the following challenges: 1. Changing **global economic conditions** post the **decline of communism** in Eastern Europe (drop in aid available to developing countries). This forced a **rethink** on India’s own **economic strategy** (inspired by the Soviet model) and the need to align with the **emerging global economic consensus**. 2. **Balance of Payment crisis (1990-91)** caused due to trade imbalances, declining remittances post- Gulf war etc. This triggered a sharp **decline in the forex reserves** (import cover declined to 2-3 weeks). 3. a) Progressive deterioration in **macro-economic fundamentals** (fiscal deficit, persistent inflation) led to a **downgrade in credit ratings** (made external borrowing costlier); b) overhanging effects of post- independence economic policies **(industrial licensing, production controls, import substitution**) undermined India’s **economic competitiveness** (low technological base of manufacturing, subscale businesses). 4. a) Pervasive inefficiencies in the **public sector** due to lack of effective **competition** from the private sector; b) myriad **bureaucratic frameworks** (permissions, inspection) giving rise to problems like **rent-** **seeking, red-tapism**. The key **objectives** of the economic reforms of 1991: 1. a) Resolution of BoP** situation through **foreign exchange reforms (**devaluation of rupee, rupee convertibility**); b) liberalization of trade policy** to enhance **competitiveness** of domestic manufacturing (new technologies) and develop India’s **consumer market.**** 2. a) Macro-economic stabilization** by restoring **fiscal discipline** (containing government expenditure and raising revenue);** b) **rapid industrial development** through de-regulation (abolition of licensing requirements, removal of price controls). 3. a) Financial sector reforms** (private banks, FDI in banking) to expand the **resource base** of banks and **ease credit access**;** b) development of a broad-based **capital market** in the country (permitting foreign institutional investors); c) **strengthening capital market regulations** (statutory status to the SEBI). 4. a) Taxation reforms (**lower rates, procedural simplification) to encourage **savings** and promote **voluntary disclosure of income;**** b) indirect tax reforms to create a **common national market** for goods and services. 5. Reducing the size of the ‘**bloated public sector’ (**privatization) and enhancing its **efficiency** (managerial autonomy). The economic reforms of 1991 laid the foundation for India's transformation, but the journey towards a **'Viksit** **Bharat by 2047'** requires another package of reforms. **Reforms 2.0** (technology upgradation, digitization, land reforms, etc.) need to aim at achieving structural overhaul of India’s economy and be guided by the principles of **inclusivity, sustainability** and **dynamism.** ***(407 words)***

• In the body, elaborate on the various policy instruments available to RBI for regulating money supply in the economy.
• Next, explain why it is termed as the ‘lender of last resort’.
• Conclude by highlighting the significance of RBI in ensuring financial stability and safeguarding depositors' interests. | | --- | The Reserve Bank of India **(RBI)** is the **Central banking authority** in India, established under the **RBI Act, 1934.** Its **key objective**, among others, is to maintain **price stability** while **supporting economic growth**. Different **policy instruments** are available to the RBI for regulating money supply in the economy, as discussed: 1. **Quantitative measures** (alter the money supply in the economy directly) a) Altering **reserve ratios** like **CRR** (4% in Feb 2025), SLR (18% in Feb 2025) which impacts **cash** **in circulation** and **credit availability**. For instance, a reduction of CRR/ SLR is likely to boost money supply in the economy. b) i) **Liquidity Adjustment Facility** (LAF) instruments like **Repo (**6.25% in Feb 2025**), Reverse** **repo rates (**3.35% in Feb 2025) and **Standing Deposit Facility** (6% in Feb 2025). They primarily help the RBI maintain **short-term liquidity** by injecting or absorbing funds in the banking system. ii) **long-term** liquidity needs are met through **Long-Term Repo Operations (**LTROs**)** which provide 1-3-year loans to banks. c) Other mechanism like i) **Bank rate** (6.5% in Feb 2025) when **no collateral** is involved (lending occurs through discounting bills of exchange); ii) **Marginal Standing Facility** (6.5% in Feb 2025) when banks are short of securities above SLR limit; iii) **Open Market Operations** (to inject durable liquidity in the banking system (e.g. Operation Twist 2019) and **Market** **Stabilization Schemes.** 2. **Qualitative Measure**s (alter the money supply **indirectly**) a) i) **Credit rationing** by fixing limits to certain sectors, e.g. CRAR framework, Priority Sector Lending (PSL) norms; ii) varying **margin requirements** for different sectors. b) i) Regulation of **consumer credit** through adjusting minimum down payment and period of repayment; ii) **moral suasion** to make banks adhere to its policies and directives. c) **Direct action** like placing under Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) Framework (Allahabad Bank) or imposing **moratorium on lending (**Yes Bank). RBI is termed as the '**lender of last resort**' because it can extend **credit to a bank** (that is solvent but faces temporary liquidity challenges) when **no one else is willing** to lend to it. For e.g., RBI extended Rs **60000-crore** **credit line** to **Yes Bank** during the 2020 crisis. Thus, the RBI employs a **mix of quantitative and qualitative instruments** to regulate the money supply and ensure financial stability. As the **lender of last resort**, its role is to provide emergency **liquidity to solvent bank**s facing crises, safeguarding depositors’ interests and the banking system. ***(397 words)***

questions.questionText: Explain the concept of ‘inclusive growth’ and outline the key measures taken by the government towards  achieving it.
questions.subject: Science & Technology

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce your answer by defining inclusive growth.
• In the body, first explain the concept by listing its key attributes.
• Next, outline the key measures taken by the government towards achieving it.
• Conclude the answer by highlighting the significance of inclusive growth in Amrit Kaal. | | --- | **UNDP defines** inclusive growth as the **process and the outcome** where all groups of people have **participated in** **growth and have benefited** equitably from it. Following are the key characteristics of inclusive growth: **1.** a) **Broad-based growth** that is spatially distributed (rural-urban) and sectorally diversified (primary, secondary, tertiary sectors); b) pro-poor orientation** addressing income disparities through productive employment generation.** **2.** a) **Equality of opportunity** across social divides (gender, caste, religion); b) participatory development** involving beneficiaries in economic **planning and implementation**;** c) systemic resilience** building and **inter-generational** sustainability (climate resilience, disaster preparedness).** The government has taken several **measures towards achieving it.** They are discussed below: 1. a) **Enhanced participation** of marginalized communities in governance through **mandatory** **representation** (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam) and **reserved executive positions** (SC/ST Sarpanch reservations); b) **institutional mechanisms** for equitable access (TRIFED, Stand Up India) facilitating **long-** **term empowerment**; c) affirmative action** in public employment (4% reservation for persons with disabilities).** 2. a) Food and nutrition security** through targeted interventions (NFSA, POSHAN Abhiyan);** b) **human** **capital development** via **educational advancement** (RTE 2009, SSA), **healthcare strengthening** (AB- PMJAY, NMHP), and **skill enhancement** (PMKVY); c) **employment generation** through **productive** **opportunities** (ELI) and **entrepreneurship support** (MUDRA, Start Up India). 3. a) Economic empowerment** through **financial inclusion** (Jan Dhan Yojana), **enhanced credit access** (SHG-BLP, KCC), and **social security expansion** (APY);** b) Infrastructure development** for **balanced** **regional growth** (PMGSY) and **accelerated economic expansion** (capex allocation of Rs. 11.21 lakh crore for FY26);** c) redistributive policies** addressing **income inequality** (progressive taxation) and establishing **income parity** (abolition of privy purse, Kisan Samman Nidhi).** 4. a) Digital inclusion initiatives** (Digital India mission, BharatNet, Common Service Centres);** b) robust** **DPI** ensuring universal access to digital services (UPI ecosystem);** c) cross-sectoral growth promotion** (RKVY, Make in India);** d) quality of life enhancement** (JJM, PMAY);** e) sustainable development** promoting **inter-generational equity** (renewable energy transition, Net Zero by 2070).** **The vision of Viksit Bharat, in Amrit Kaal** would remain unrealized without ensuring **inclusive growth.** Thus, it becomes imperative to prioritize **Sabka Sath Sabka Vikas Sabka Prayas** to fulfill the constitutional mandate of creating a **welfare state.** **(341 words)** **Additional Reading:** **What is Inclusive Growth |ForumIAS** **A Lesson from IIT | Envisioning frameworks for inclusive growth of India through ‘techno-social’ entrepreneurship informed by UN** **SDGs | Education News - The Indian Express** **TRIFED:** Tribal Co-operative Marketing Development Federation of India; **NFSA:** National Food Security Act; **POSHAN:** Prime Minister's Overarching Scheme for Holistic Nourishment; **RTE Act:** Right to Education Act; **SSA:** Sarva Shisha Abhiyan; **AB-PMJAY:** Ayushman Bharat- Pradhan Mantri Jan Aarogya Yojana; **NMHP:** National Mental Health Programme; **PMKVY:** Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana; **ELI:** Employment-Linked Incentive**; MUDRA:** Micro Units Development and Refinancing Agency; **SHG-BLP:** Self Help Group- Bank Linkage Programme; **KCC:** Kisan Credit Card; **APY:** Atal Pension Yojana; **PMGSY:** Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana; **DPI:** Digital Public Infrastructure**; UPI:** Unified Payment Interface; **RKVY:** Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana; **JJM:** Jal Jeevan Mission**; PMAY:** Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana

| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by giving a brief background of the budget exercise in India and its parts.
• In the body, first distinguish between capital and revenue budget.
• Next, explain the components of both these budgets.
• Conclude by underlining the significance of this distinction. | | --- | **Article 112** of the Constitution mandates the **President** to lay the Budget (**Annual Financial Statement**) of the Union Government **before Parliament**, for every financial year. It comprises **capital budget** and **revenue budget**. The table below discusses the **differences** between them: **Capital Budget** **Revenue Budget** 1. a) Statement of estimated **capital receipts** and 1. a) Statement of estimated **revenues receipts** and **capital expenditure**; b) deals with **investment, asset** **revenue expenditure**; b) deals with **current income** **creation, and liabilities.** **and expenditure** of the government. 2. a) Nature of transactions covered by it is **non-**2. a) Nature of transactions covered by it is **recurring**; **recurring**; b) **high multiplier effect** as the b) **low multiplier effect** as the components under it components under it boosts **employment**, are mainly **consumption-oriented**. **infrastructure**, and economic growth. 3. a) Influence on the **day-to-day functioning of the** 3. a) Influence on broader **development objectives** **government;** b) used to calculate the **revenue** and **economic growth;** b) no such fiscal metric** **deficit (**revenue expenditure-revenue receipts). exists for capital account, although it affects **fiscal** **deficit.**** **Components of capital budget** **1.** **Capital Receipts:** Consist of market borrowings by the government, borrowings from RBI and commercial banks, loans from international organizations, recovery from loans granted by the government etc. **2.** **Capital Expenditure:** Consists spending on acquiring assets (land, buildings, machinery etc), investments in PSUs, investments in infrastructure projects, loans granted by the government etc. **Components of revenue budget** **1.** **Revenue receipts** a) **Tax receipts:** Consist of the proceeds of the taxes and other duties levied by the government. E.g. GST (indirect tax), personal income tax (direct tax), customs duty. **b)** **Non-tax receipts:** Consist of interest receipts, dividends, profits on investment etc. Also includes fees from services rendered by the government and grants-in-aid. **2.** **Revenue expenditure:** a) Consist of expenditure that does not result in creation of assets. E.g. salaries, pensions, interest payments; b) was earlier further classified into **plan** and **non-plan expenditure (**abolished in 2017**).** The **distinction** between capital and revenue budget is a **constitutional mandate** (Article 112 (2)). Simultaneously, it helps provide **clarity on how public monies are being utilised** (whether for immediate operational needs or long-term asset creation), thereby ensuring **transparency in fiscal management. questions.questionText: What do you understand by agroecology? Identify and discuss its key principles.
questions.subject: Economy

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** |
| --- |

Approach - Introduce the answer with a brief description of agroecology. In the body, identify and discuss its key

principles with relevant examples. Conclude by mentioning the significance of agroecology for the future.

Agroecology is an integrated approach that incorporates ecological principles and social equity in agriculture and

food systems with the goal to build greater resilience,resource-use efficiency and overall sustainability.

The principles of agroecology incorporate ecological, social, and economic factors into food production and

consumption. Some of the key principles are discussed below.

1. a) Recycling: Use of local renewable resources, closing nutrient and biomass cycles (as far as possible) ;

   b) Input reduction: reduce or eliminate dependency on synthetic/external inputs (e.g. Zero Budget Natural

Farming); c) Soil health: securing and enhancing soil health by managing organic matter and increasing soil

biological activity for improved plant growth (e.g. Soil Health Card); d) Animal health: ensuring animal

health and welfare (e.g. National Livestock Mission).

2. a) Biodiversity: Maintaining and enhancing species diversity, functional diversity and genetic resources

within the agroecosystem (Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers Rights Act); b) Synergy: Enhancing

positive ecological interaction, synergy, and complementarity amongst the elements of agroecosystems

(plants, animals, trees, soil, water).

3. a) Economic diversification: Diversifying on-farm incomes, providing small-scale farmers with greater

financial independence (e.g. integrated farming systems); b) co-creation of knowledge: co-creation and

horizontal sharing of knowledge including local and scientific innovation, especially through farmer-to-

farmer exchange (e.g. NADEP* composting); c) social values and diets: build food systems based on

culture, identity, tradition, social and gender equity of local communities that provide healthy, diversified,

seasonally and culturally appropriate diets.

4. a)Fairness: Supporting dignified and robust livelihoods, especially small-scale food producers, based on

fair trade, fair employment and fair treatment of intellectual property rights; b) connectivity: developing

fair and short distribution networks and re-embedding food systems into local economies.

5. a) Land and natural resource governance: recognizing and supporting family farmers, smallholders etc as

sustainable managers and guardians of natural and genetic resources; b) Participation: social organization

and greater participation in decision-making to support decentralized governance and local adaptive

management of agricultural and food systems (e.g. FPOs).

Agroecology offers a sustainable alternative to the challenges of industrial agriculture, including food insecurity,

climate change, and social inequality. A gradual, evidence-based adoption of agroecological practices—without

disrupting current levels of food production—presents a balanced path forward. (326 words)

*NADEP: Narayan Deotao Pandharipande method of composting

Additional reading:

Overview | Agroecology Knowledge Hub | Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

questions.questionText: India’s BioE3 Policy (Biotechnology for Economy, Environment, and Employment) is a strategic step towards building a sustainable bioeconomy. Examine the key mechanisms through which the policy seeks to strengthen the biomanufacturing ecosystem.
questions.subject: Science & Technology

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce your answer by giving a brief background of the policy.
• In the body of your answer, examine important mechanisms intended to strengthen the biomanufacturing ecosystem.
• Conclude by highlighting the alignment of the policy with the broader national objectives. | | --- | In August 2024, the Union Cabinet approved India's BioE3 Policy (Biotechnology for Economy, Environment, and Employment) as a strategic initiative for fostering high performance (advanced) biomanufacturing. The policy envisages the following key mechanisms to strengthen the biomanufacturing ecosystem in the country: 1. a)Creation of Biomanufacturing Hubs and Biofoundries across India to facilitate the scaling up of production processes and efficient manufacture of bio-based products; b)co-locating these hubs with existing research and infrastructure centers to foster innovation and accelerate the translation and commercialization of biotechnological advancements. 2. a)Integration of AI technologies into biomanufacturing processes through the establishment of Bio-AI Hubs; b)these hubs serve as centers of excellence, fostering interdisciplinary collaboration among academia, industry, and research institutions; c) they enable acceleration of data analysis, optimize production processes, and enhance decision-making in areas such as genomics, proteomics, and synthetic biology. 3. a)Introduction of the Bio-RIDE framework, which integrates biotechnology research and entrepreneurship under a cohesive policy structure; b)development of a skilled workforce through developing specialised training programs and higher education programs/curricula, in collaboration with industry leaders. 4. a)Focus on six thematic sectors of national importance viz. (i) bio-based chemicals and enzymes, (ii)precision biotherapeutics, (iii)climate resilient agriculture, (iv)functional foods, (v) carbon capture and utilization, (vi)futuristic marine and space research); b) the policy aims at driving innovation and commercialization in these sectors, which are critical to India's economic and environmental goals. Overall, the BioE3 policy aligns with the goal of a ‘Net Zero’ economy by 2070 and the vision of the ‘LiFE mission.’ It is expected to steer India on the path of accelerated ‘Green Growth’ by promoting ‘Circular Bioeconomy’. The Policy will foster sustainability, innovation, and responsiveness to global challenges and lays down the Bio-vision for Viksit Bharat. (270 words) Additional reading: BioE3 Policy Initiative |ForumIAS Centre’s new BioE3 policy: How can biotechnology be harnessed for economic development? | Explained News - The Indian Express Extra marks/content differentiation: 1. Quotes: • “As biology meets technology, biotechnology emerges as the architect of groundbreaking scientific innovations: from cellular mastery to societal progress. • From the lab to the field, from cells to societies, biotechnology carves the path from scientific insight to revolutionary applications.” 2. International Best practices: The European Union Bioeconomy Strategy aims to boost innovation and support European companies in making a success of the green transition. The strategy is expected to make EU businesses more competitive and increase green jobs – without damaging nature. The main goals of the strategy are: • Ensuring the long-term competitiveness of the EU bioeconomy and investment security. Identifying measures to scale up and commercialise existing and emerging biotech solutions and bio-based products. • Increasing resource-efficient and circular use of biological resources. Transforming the use and valuation of biomass resources, prioritizing extended high-value applications while encouraging industries and consumers to embrace circular practices. • Securing the competitive and sustainable supply of biomass, both domestically and from outside the EU. Strengthening the role of primary producers, generating wealth in rural areas by creating jobs and diversifying incomes for foresters and farmers and rewarding them for the preservation of ecosystems. • Positioning the EU in the rapidly expanding international market for bio-based materials, biomanufacturing, biochemicals, and agri-food and biotech sectors. This will be done, in particular, by steering existing foreign policy mechanisms.

questions.questionText: Discuss the role of Dr. Verghese Kurien in revolutionising India’s dairy sector and empowering rural communities.
questions.subject: Science & Technology

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce your answer by giving a brief description about Dr.
• Kurien’s legacy as the Father of India’s White Revolution.
• In the body, highlight the pivotal role played by him in revolutionizing India’s dairy sector and empowering rural communities.
• Conclude your answer by mentioning some of the accolades earned by him. | | --- | Dr. Verghese Kurien is considered the key architect behind India’s transformation from a milk-deficit nation into the world’s largest milk producer. He is popularly known as the Father of the White Revolution in India. The role of Dr. Verghese Kurien in revolutionising India’s dairy sector and empowering rural communities: 1. a) Played a pivotal role in transforming the Kaira District Cooperative Milk Producers’ Union Limited (KDCMPUL) into the successful enterprise known as Amul; b) infused technology in the supply chain (standard fat checking machine, pasteurization, powder production, cooling and packaging units); c)realised the importance of branding in dairy sector and came out with the name “Amul”(registered in 1957), which has served as a model for cooperatives in several parts of the world. 2. a)Championed and institutionalized the three tier structure- Village societies, District Union and State federations; b) established systems ensuring farmers received remunerative prices; c) as the founding chairman of the National Dairy Development Board(NDDB) led the replication of the “Anand model” nationwide. 3. a)Launched “Operation Flood” in 1970 under NDDB; b)catapulted India to self-sufficiency and the world’s top milk producer by 1998; c)milk output surged from ~23 MT (1968–69) to ~239 MT (2023-24),per‑capita consumption nearly quadrupled (124gm/day in 1950-51 to 471gm/day in 2023-24). 4. a)Founded Institute of Rural Management Anand(IRMA) in 1979 for cooperative management education and to train rural managers; b)initiated edible-oil cooperative (“Dhara” in 1979) and and the Mother Dairy fruit and vegetable project in Delhi (aimed to provide a direct link between fruit and vegetable growers and consumers). 5. a)Over 85,000 village dairy co-operatives formed inspired from Amul model, empowering 15 million farmers (FAO report on Dairy Development in India); b)promoted inclusion of women in dairy cooperatives, contributing to economic independence and social mobility(e.g.,Mahila Dairy Cooperative Societies). 6. a)Contributed to improved animal health through cooperative veterinary services; b) contributed significantly to improved nutrition in rural areas; c) pioneered a model of decentralised development through localising production, processing, and profits; d)strengthened social cohesion by breaking caste and religious distinctions. Dr.Kurien’s main contribution has been as an institution builder,empowering people to develop themselves as he believed that people are the greatest asset of a country. His contribution has earned him many accolades including Padma Vibhushan (1999) and ‘Ramon Magsaysay award (1963). (364 words) Additional reading: Indian agriculture needs a Verghese Kurien -ForumIAS Blog Verghese Kurien, the engineer who 'dairied' to dream and ushered in the White Revolution https://forumias.com/blog/tribhuvandas-patel/ Extra marks/content differentiation: 1. Quote: • “Milk is the only commodity which has to be collected twice a day, every day of the year. Thus, cooperatives are the only logical system for the dairy industry. About 85% of the industry in the US, Denmark and Australia is run by cooperatives. No other system will work for milk.”- Dr. Verghese Kurien • “Dr Kurien's greatest contribution was to give a position of pre-eminence to the farmer".- former PM Dr. Manohan Singh 2. Government initiatives: • The Ministry of Cooperation has launched cooperative-led "White Revolution 2.0” aimed at expanding cooperative coverage, employment generation and women's empowerment. • Its objective is to “increase the milk procurement from dairy cooperatives by 50% from the present level over next five years by providing market access to dairy farmers in uncovered areas and increasing the share of dairy cooperatives in the organised sector. • For the above purpose, the Ministry of Cooperation has envisaged to set up 75,000 new Dairy Cooperative Societies (DCSs) in uncovered panchayats/villages and strengthen 46,422 existing DCSs. • These DCSs will be provided market linkage either by expanding the existing milk routes or by creating new milk routes. NDDB will coordinate various activities related to White Revolution 2.0. • Women play an indispensable role in India’s dairy sector performing important work related to milking, feeding, managing cattle and ensuring animal health. • Nearly 70% of the workforce in dairy farming consists of women, yet their contribution often remains undervalued due to the unorganized nature of the sector. Women led dairy cooperatives have emerged as powerful tools for their empowerment.

questions.questionText: What is gene therapy? What makes it a better treatment option than the conventional approaches?
questions.subject: Science & Technology

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by giving a brief explanation about gene therapy.
• In the body, discuss its advantages over conventional approaches.
• Next, mention the associated concerns and challenges.
• Conclude by emphasizing the need for adherence to regulatory framework. | | --- | According to the ICMR, Gene Therapy refers to the process of introduction, removal or change in content of an individual’s genetic material to treat a disease and achieve long term cure. It can work by following mechanisms: 1. Replacing a disease-causing gene with a healthy copy of the gene. 2. Inactivating a disease-causing gene that is not functioning properly. 3. Introducing a new or modified gene into the body to help treat a disease. Advantages of gene therapy over other conventional treatments are as follows: 1. a) Ability to address the root cause of the disease (repairing faulty genes). Conventional approaches usually offer only symptomatic treatment; b) greater promise to cure genetic disorders and rare diseases (e.g. OTOF gene therapy for restoring hearing loss). 2. a) Long-lasting benefits, offered by modified genes (e.g. CAR-T Cell therapy uses the body's own immune system to fight cancerous cells). Conventional approaches, however, need regular administration (e.g. insulin injections); b) lesser chances of disease relapse as compared to conventional approaches (e.g. cancer recurrence after chemotherapy). 3. a) Improved treatment efficiency (can be targeted to specific cells- e.g. CRISPR CaS 9); b) reduced risk of harmful side effects (e.g. hair loss after radiotherapy); c) ease of delivery of treatments (e.g. through injections). This can help avoid the complex conventional approaches (e.g. invasive surgeries for brain tumours). However, it also poses the following risks/challenges: 1. a) Immunological barriers (e.g. rejection of ‘foreign genes’); b) risk of unintended mutations (e.g. off target events in CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing) that can pose long-term side effects; c) ineffectiveness for complex, multifactorial diseases where the underlying genetic cause is unknown (e.g. Alzheimer's). 2. a) Likely to deepen existing health care divide (prohibitive costs, pharmaceutical monopolies); b) concerns due to technological development outpacing regulatory oversight; c) ethical considerations arising from artificial genetic selection and human intervention in “godly affairs” (e.g. germline editing to produce designer babies by Chinese biophysicist He Jiankui). India’s first home-grown gene therapy for cancer was launched at IIT Bombay (April 2024), marking a significant breakthrough in treating complex diseases like cancer. However, continuous advancements under a robust regulatory framework (ICMR's 2019 guidelines), while driving affordability (cell and gene therapy mission mooted by the Principal Scientific Advisor), are essential to address the associated concerns. (382 words) Additional reading: Explained: What is gene therapy? How is DNA used to treat genetic disorders? - Times of India Extra marks/content differentiation: 1. Quotes: • “The advance of genetic engineering makes it quite conceivable that we will begin to design our own evolutionary progress.” — Isaac Asimov • “I think the ethics and morals of genetic engineering are very complicated. It intrigues me.” — Roger Spottiswoode 2. Case study: Scientists from the CSIR-Institute of Genomics and Integrative Biology, New Delhi, have developed an enhanced genome-editing system that can modify DNA more precisely and more efficiently than existing CRISPR-based technologies. To enhance it without compromising its specificity, researchers led by Debojyoti Chakraborty and Souvik Maiti at CSIR-IGIB modified and engineered new versions of FnCas9. The researchers tinkered with amino acids in FnCas9 that recognise and interact with the PAM sequence on the host genome. By doing this, we increase the binding affinity of the Cas protein with the PAM sequence. The Cas9 can then sit on the DNA in a stronger configuration, and your gene editing becomes much more effective.The researchers also engineered the enhanced FnCas9 to be more flexible and edit regions of the genome that are otherwise harder to access.Experiments to measure enzyme activity showed that enhanced FnCas9 cut target DNA at a higher rate compared to unmodified FnCas9.

questions.questionText: What are marine heat waves? Throw light on its impact on marine ecosystem and coastal communities.
questions.subject: Environment

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • In the introduction, explain marine heat waves briefly.
• In the body, throw light on their impact on marine ecosystems and coastal communities.
• Conclude by highlighting some measures for mitigation and adaptation. | | --- | Marine heat waves (MHWs) are extreme weather events linked with marine areas. They occur where the surface temperature of a particular region of the sea rises by 3 to 4 ℃ above the average temperature for at least five days. Two main drivers of marine heat waves are: 1. Surface heat flux: Heating of sea surface due to presence of an atmospheric high-pressure system above a region of water for an extended period. 2. Advection: Movement of warmer waters into the region by ocean currents. They have severe impact on marine ecosystems and coastal communities, as discussed: 1. a) Disruption of food webs due to invasive alien species, harmful algal blooms; b) amplify the risk of other ocean stressors like acidification, deoxygenation; c) can cause incidents of mass mortalities. This can happen when the threshold for thermal tolerance is breached or due to increase in hypoxic zones e.g. (“fish kills” in Gulf of Thailand and Gulf of Mexico). 2. a) Loss of ocean biodiversity due to habitat destruction (kelp forests, seagrass meadows, coral reefs are most sensitive to MHWs); b) forced changes in species’ behaviour (altering migration patterns). This increases the risk of harm to marine species (e.g. increase in whale and dolphin stranding in the South Pacific Ocean in January 2024). 3. a) Impact on aquaculture and fisheries (death or reduced productivity of economically important species like lobsters and snow crabs). It has a cascading effect on livelihoods and food security; b) harms regional tourism. 4. a) Disruption of water cycle (increased evaporation). This can cause hydrological (floods, droughts) and meteorological (wildfires, heatwaves) disasters on the land; b) frequent MHWs in the Indian Ocean is altering the patterns of monsoon rains (IITM study). This can severely impact agriculture and allied activities, for e.g. MHWs in Bay of Bengal in June 2023 caused extreme rainfall in usually arid north-western part of India. 5. a) Can ‘supercharge’ the heat and moisture exchanges between sea and air, which could intensify tropical cyclones (e.g. Cyclone Remal). This can have devastating consequences for coastal communities (e.g. loss of life and property) c) contributes to sea-level rise (due to thermal expansion of water), which can lead to coastal erosion, flooding, etc. An analysis published in Nature Climate Change has pointed out a 240 per cent increase in the average number of marine heatwave (MHW) days in the summers of 2023-24. It is important to develop better response plans and adaptation and intervention approaches as they intensify under climate change. Measures to reduce global carbon emissions and slow down ocean warming can counteract their impact and build ocean resilience. (432 words) Additional reading: https://forumias.com/blog/marine-heatwaves-mhws/ Rapid warming over last 2 years likely caused 240% increase in marine heatwaves globally: Study Extra marks/content differentiation: Previous studies have shown that the Indian Ocean has warmed at a rate of 1.2°C per century during 1950-2020. Between 2020 and 2100, climate models predict warming at a rate of 1.7°C-3.8°C per century. The effects are expected to be more pronounced in the northwestern Indian Ocean including the Arabian Sea.

questions.questionText: What is disaster resilience? How is it determined? Describe various elements of a resilience framework. Also mention the global targets of Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015-2030).
questions.subject: Environment

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer with a brief definition of disaster resilience.
• In the body, first explain how it is determined.
• Next, describe the various elements of a resilience framework.
• Lastly, mention the global targets of Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015-30).
• Conclude by highlighting the significance of recent changes in the Disaster Management Act for disaster resilience. | | --- | According to UNDRR, disaster resilience means the ability of communities to anticipate, accommodate, and recover from disasters while maintaining essential functions. It is determined by the degree to which the social system is capable of enhancing its capacity to learn from past disasters. This leads to better future protection and improved risk reduction measures. A disaster resilient framework consists of diverse elements as discussed: 1. a) Hazard identification, exposure mapping and vulnerability assessment across social, economic and environmental dimensions; b) planning for the disaster through mitigation (earthquake proofing of building codes) and adaptation measures (drought resilient crop varieties). 2. a) Infrastructure evaluation, especially critical infrastructure (health, communication); b) development of infrastructural (cyclone shelters) and institutional capacity (National Disaster Management Plan); c) capacity building of the community (awareness generation, training, knowledge creation through NIDM) 3. a) Augmentation of the resource base of the economy (financial, technological) to deal with disaster comprehensively; b) ensuring availability of human capital (trained personnel, social networks, social cohesion and trust, local leadership); c) strengthening social security architecture (e.g. risk coverage through insurance). 4. a) Mounting an effective response to the disaster through a whole of society (civil society organizations, volunteer groups) and a whole of government approach (multi-agency coordination); b) effective rehabilitation and recovery from the disaster (Build Back Better approach). The Sendai Framework is the successor of the Hyogo Framework for Action and outlines 7 global targets to be achieved by 2030: I. Substantially reduce: (a) Global disaster mortality (lower average per 100,000 global mortality). (b)The number of affected people (lower average global figure per 100,000). (c) Direct disaster economic loss in relation to global GDP. (d) Damage to critical infrastructure and disruption of basic services (health and education) II. Substantially increase: (e) Number of countries with national and local DRR strategies by 2020. (f) International cooperation to developing countries to complement their national actions. (g) Availability of and access to multi-hazard early warning systems and disaster risk information and assessments. The Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025 marks a significant step towards mainstreaming disaster resilience in development planning. It is expected to go a long way in building a disaster-resilient Bharat. (326 words) Additional reading: Strengthening telecom networks ensures resilience during disasters |ForumIAS Why India needs to build disaster resilience in its critical infrastructure | Explained News - The Indian Express Extra marks/content differentiation: 1. Quotes: “When it comes to disaster management, a proactive approach is always better than a reactive one”- Prime Minister Narendra Modi 2. International Best Practices: In Chile, innovative stormwater management systems and alluvial flood protection schemes have been designed to address flood issues by integrating future climate projections into their design. These systems incorporate updated geotechnical, structural, and hydraulic information combined with natural water retention methods, effectively reducing the impact of climate-induced flood events in the cities. 3. Best practices from India: Real-time monitoring and early warning systems such as cloud-based E-Abhas software have been developed by NHPC Limited. They provide timely warnings against flood risks, enabling governments and communities to take appropriate actions. The implementation of the EWS has significantly enhanced disaster preparedness and response capabilities in regions vulnerable to floods.
